description:
Wesam Saad opens the End Times course by asking why Christians avoid studying the end times. He identifies reactions against date setting, the complexity of competing interpretations, preoccupation with present life and fear of division. He challenges the assumption that future hope has little bearing on spiritual growth now. His aim is to teach what the church understands Scripture to say while encouraging mature fellowship with Christians who reach different conclusions. Conviction should coexist with humility, love and a willingness to learn.

The recording includes small-group discussion and participant reports about hope, resurrection, judgment, rewards and daily conduct. These contributions remain distinct from Saad's own teaching. He then outlines a course moving through the kingdom of God, the millennium, the rapture and tribulation, Christ's return, final judgment, the eternal state and rewards. This is a proposed teaching outline rather than proof that every planned session was recorded. Opening with the blessing associated with reading, hearing and heeding Revelation, he invites questions that help the whole group understand. He also asks that detailed disputes be taken up separately when they would overwhelm the class. The intended outcome is encouragement, holiness and a life that points others to Christ.

questions.question: Why does Saad say Christians often avoid end-times teaching?
questions.answer: He identifies four recurring reasons: reacting against false date setters, feeling intimidated by complex disagreements, concentrating on present life and fearing division. He questions whether these justify leaving biblical teaching unexplored.

questions.question: Does this introduction encourage predicting a date for Christ's return?
questions.answer: No. Saad criticises attempts to specify dates and the embarrassment caused by failed predictions. He argues that rejecting date setting should lead to careful study rather than avoiding the whole subject.

questions.question: How does he connect future hope with spiritual life now?
questions.answer: Saad challenges the idea that studying the future distracts from loving and enjoying Christ today. He intends the course to encourage holy conduct, lasting priorities and a life that influences others for Christ.

questions.question: How should Christians treat believers who interpret these passages differently?
questions.answer: Saad calls for loving fellowship and humility alongside personal conviction. He says a Christian may hold a different view while recognising another believer as deeply godly. Different conclusions need not become a reason for hostility.

questions.question: How should the participant reports in this recording be understood?
questions.answer: They are small-group responses within the class, not all statements by Saad. Participants discuss hope, resurrection, judgment, rewards and practical priorities; the recording also includes informal comments and humour. Their reports should retain that attribution.

questions.question: What does Saad plan to cover in the course?
questions.answer: He outlines the kingdom of God and the millennium, the rapture and tribulation, Christ's return, the great white throne, the eternal state and rewards. He expects some topics to take several sessions. This outline states his intentions without establishing a complete recording inventory.

questions.question: What role will questions and differences of interpretation have?
questions.answer: Saad invites questions so that he can address the class's concerns. He plans to explain the church's understanding and sometimes compare other views, while moving highly technical disputes to a separate conversation when they would leave most participants behind.

questions.question: What outcome does he want beyond gaining theological information?
questions.answer: He wants the teaching to encourage and edify the class, deepen holy living and help them bring Christ's influence into the world. He explicitly rejects using the course simply to display theological superiority.
